content: Magnesium sulfate, available in oral and topical forms, is a saline laxative approved by the FDA for the treatment of occasional constipation. It typically induces bowel movements within 30 minutes to 6 hours after administration. Additionally, it can be used externally as a soaking aid for minor sprains and bruises. For oral use, the recommended dosage for adults and children aged 12 years and older is 2 to 6 level teaspoons (10 to 30 grams) daily. For children aged 6 to under 12 years, the dosage is 1 to 2 level teaspoons (5 to 10 grams) daily. Children under 6 years of age should only use this product under the guidance of a physician. The dose should be dissolved in 8 ounces of water, and lemon juice may be added to improve the taste. It can be taken as a single daily dose or divided into multiple doses. It is important not to exceed the recommended daily dosage and to drink a full glass (8 ounces) of liquid with each dose. For soaking purposes, dissolve 2 cupfuls of magnesium sulfate per gallon of water. This solution can be applied using bandages or toweling for 30 minutes up to three times a day, or it can be used as a soak or in a bath. Warm water is recommended for optimal results. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of magnesium sulfate in both adults and pediatric patients. Similarly, there is limited data on its contraindications, clinical trial experience, postmarketing experience, drug interactions, and specific population use, including pregnancy, nursing mothers, pediatric, geriatric, gender, racial, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, and immunocompromised patients. Warnings for soaking include discontinuing use and consulting a physician if prompt relief is not achieved or if signs of infection are present. Individuals with diabetes should avoid hot or warm soaks unless advised by a physician. The product should be kept out of reach of children. Before use, individuals with kidney disease, a magnesium-restricted diet, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or a sudden change in bowel habits persisting for more than two weeks should consult a doctor. Additionally, those who have already used a laxative for more than one week should seek medical advice. In case of overdose, immediate medical attention or contact with a Poison Control Center is necessary. If pregnant or breastfeeding, consult a healthcare professional before use. There is no established guidance on the interaction of magnesium sulfate with alcohol, so patients should discuss potential effects with their doctor. The pharmacology of magnesium sulfate, including its mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology, is not well-documented in the drug label. Similarly, there is limited information on its clinical studies, storage, administration, monitoring, IV compatibility, and patient counseling information. There is also no specific guidance on its use in females of reproductive potential, males, or immunocompromised patients. Magnesium sulfate is categorized as Pregnancy Category D by the FDA, indicating potential risks to the fetus. However, there is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on its use during pregnancy. For labor and delivery, as well as nursing mothers, consultation with a healthcare professional is advised. Finally, there is no established information regarding look-alike drug names for magnesium sulfate in the drug label.
